note_tweet.text:
deleting the product
it's funny how you can sometimes tell if a team culture is dysfunctional just by looking at how their app is laid out. behind every feature, or tab in a sidebar likely lies a PM or someone responsible for an OKR.

the problem is when individual performance is measured by these metrics. it becomes the singular focus of the responsible person to make those numbers look good, since it determines whether they get rewarded or axed, even if it comes at the detriment of the overall quality of the product. this is why you mostly see features get added, but rarely removed. if you own a feature, then it being removed feels like an aura loss.

this is even worse in the agentic era when the cost to add features has become so low. you can simply will a new feature into existence overnight and add another tab. but users will notice that you ship your org chart.

teams that make people play silly games under the guise of performance management rarely build great products.

to build a great product you need to first fix your culture

note_tweet.text:
it's easy to fall into the trap of micromanaging your agents instead of correcting the environment that shapes its behavior. 

pstack 0.15.9 now ships a new /correct skill: if you keep correcting agents for the same mistakes, it finds the pattern and fixes it with architecture, types, and checks.

i like to imagine that commits rapidly flowing into the codebase are like a bonsai tree rapidly growing in whatever direction it pleases. what you want to do is not to give in to the chaos, but tame it intentionally with the right constraints

0.15.9 also has improvements to:
• /architect: now includes instructions on designing agent friendly architecture
• a new /benchmark-checklist skill based on @brendangregg's benchmarking checklist

here's a prompt you can give to grok bot to start architecting a better codebase with pstack: 

/poteto-mode create a new Project agent to refactor and rearchitect my repo so that our architecture is more agent friendly. it should use both the /correct and /architect skill to look through past commits and find the most common pitfalls that agents fall into, whether its with code quality, performance, or bugs. if relevant you can also use the /recall skill to find past conversations for context. it should make a high level plan for me to review. it should also answer its own open questions by prototyping rather than defer to me. come back to me with a plan backed by real data. once i approve the plan, use either the stack or full autopilot playbook (ask me which i want) to execute

note_tweet.text:
everything i know about managing agents i learned from the amazing programmers and computer scientists that came before

constraints in your codebase are freeing for both humans and agents! this has always been true, but if you were a small dev team you likely never had to think that deeply because you could trust your fellow programmers to write code and review well

but large companies have had to solve this problem since even before agents. because before you had agent slop, you had human slop. lots of engineers wrote bad code out of necessity (eg backend engineer forced to write frontend or reverse). the solution to this was constraints: lint rules, smarter compilers and diagnostics, high quality tests, investments into observability, and so on

the arrival of agents just means that big company problems are now everyone's problems. the good news is that none of this is really that novel: it's just good engineering

https://t.co/ykgu52qBqB

the first mile is figuring out what work you should even be doing at all. that involves connecting Bot to the different apps and services you use, so that it can grab whatever context it needs - whether it's your calendar, your CRM, slack, email, or the many other connectors available. then, the first mile begins when you combine these connections, allowing you to provide context to your bot ("look at this slack channel for new features we've built and then look through our CRM to see which  customers we should nudge") instead of micromanage it.

you can automate further by setting up routines - they let your bot do something on a schedule ("check my email every morning") or as a reaction to something ("do this whenever this slack channel has a new message"). so a new lead can kick off a whole workflow that you setup for your bot, allowing you to delegate the work you would otherwise have to do to your bot!

the last mile involves actually following through and closing the loop. one example of this is building a new feature, or fixing a bug that your customers have reported. this is where Bot can hand off tasks to Cursor - our engineering focused agents that can write code in the cloud, on their own computers.

when you've gotten the hang of this, the next thing you can try is building a loop. here's a simple example that i use daily:

1. watch this slack channel for feedback about our app
2. create a ticket for this in Linear
3. create a Cursor cloud agent to triage and reproduce the issue on its own computer, using pstack
4. if the issue clearly reproduces, put up a fix and fuzz the pull request with a small swarm of agents
5. if the fuzz has no issues, ping me on Slack, and rebase and auto-merge the PR after 1 hour unless i request changes

you can also install my bot Dr Eggbot and ask it to teach you how to setup a loop like this for yourself!

https://t.co/U1shj39y3J

i just automated our release and QA process!
using Grok Bot i made two Team Bots: sandcastle, my release manager, and poteto, my engineer bot. i added them to Slack and made a new channel for managing releases.

first i tell sandcastle that i want to do a cut. it'll DM all the contributors with links to their PRs so they know what goes in the next release and can DM the bot back if they have any blockers or objections.

sandcastle then kicks off the build, watches it automatically, and starts up an automated fuzz swarm. usually this is 10+ agents running on Grok 4.7 xhigh to run the build, click around and use it like a real user (using our verification skills and feature map), some are directed while a few are "chaos monkey" clicking things randomly to see what breaks. 

whenever it finds an issue, i tell it to @ mention my engineer bot poteto, to spin up a Cursor Project to own triaging and fixing all the high pri issues. depending on the severity i may ask it to cherry pick the fix into our release branch and cut a patch release, or if it's a pre-existing issue i still fix it but include in the next release instead

that's one more tedious task that Grok Bot now handles for our team

note_tweet.text:
something I have been thinking about is a way to approximate how well you’ve setup your codebase for agents. think of it as a thought experiment and rough heuristic, not a real number that can be compared

it’s not a fully formed idea yet, but i think there’s something to the idea of “time to (fully automated, hands off) rewrite” or ttr

as a thought experiment, lets say you decided to rewrite your code in a different language/framework/architecture. how long would it take a single engineer to do it?
 
the number itself isn’t that important, but it leads you to more questions that can help you directionally figure out how to make your codebase more legible and productive for agents. 

for example, maybe you think your ttr is high because you wouldn’t trust the final result - because your agents don’t have a way to verify their work and convince you that their output is identical in user visible behavior to the original. well, that inability is likely also a problem today and slows you and your agents down 

there’s also a more subtle question of the quality of the rewrite that would be produced. is perf better, the same, or regressed? is the code easy to delete and extend? and how much do you trust the rewritten version to be able to maintain its quality over time as PRs start flowing into it?

what do you think?

note_tweet.text:
volume does matter
look, i get it. if you were an engineer before agents came along, you're rightfully skeptical about lines of code and number of PRs being used as a metric for any kind of productivity. and i agree! or at least, i used to. for ease of explanation i will talk about this from the perspective as being an engineer on a large team of at least 50. 

volume didn't matter before because we focused on impact. you could have high impact even with a few PRs: for example you could make a one line config change and save the company millions of dollars.  

but before agents, the times where i saw volume come into the conversation were for the outliers. on the negative end you might have someone who is struggling to perform, on the other end you might have someone who was a "coding machine" archetype. a coding machine was someone who could just lock themselves in a room and emerge with a stack of PRs that solve a huge number of problems. so volume did matter, but only at the tail ends of the distribution, and combined with impact.

if you've ever worked at a large tech company before, you'll get what i mean. the thing about agents is that big tech co problems are now small-medium co problems as well. 

how do agents change this calculus? well, everyone now has the ability to become a coding machine. you have incredibly capable frontier models that can write code better than any of us, at a rate much faster than we can. in this world, if you're still producing the same number of PRs as before, why wouldn't you pause to wonder why you're not being more productive? alien intelligence is here, and yet you can't outship a human coding machine?

this brings me back to why i keep talking about trust (https://t.co/7fzYZV8LGH). if you haven't put in the work to trust your agent's output, it is very difficult to scale up your productivity. 

and yes, this approach does require more tokens, but i think about this in terms of cost per intelligence. before agents, this cost was very high - you needed to hire many software engineers with high 6 figure salaries to do the work. tokens are still expensive today, but are likely to get cheaper over time (https://t.co/gTBZx7pl14) factoring in the cost of intelligence. what looks exorbitant today will likely be affordable in 6 moths to a year. a single engineer with agents can do the work of tens if not hundreds of engineers, at a fraction of the cost.

the reality that i don't think has hit yet is that job of the software engineer has truly changed. our job is not merely to produce software any longer (well tbh it was never only about the code, but bear with me for the sake of the explanation), but the machine that writes the software. this idea of a software factory, or a Michelin kitchen as i like to call it, is still a topic of research. and it's the type of stuff i like to share, not to flex, but to show you what's possible when you put a lot of rigor into using agents at scale

note_tweet.text:
on a related note, there's been some chatter recently about software engineering skills (eg the ruby/rust/elixir drama). i'm a bit torn because while i do feel like they're software engineering principles and patterns are still important, at the same time i wonder if there will come a point in time when they just won't matter anymore. not that they're no longer useful, but that your own intuition can fill in the gaps as you use agents in an intuitive sense rather than knowing explicitly what they're doing

if that doesn't make sense, the analogy i have is the first iphone. 20 years ago you had to be a professional with expensive equipment, now just with a phone and some creativity you can film content that's compelling to a new audience. i don't know if there's a term for this but i want to call it "skill compression". where what used to be gatekept and prohibitive to experts becomes accessible to a new audience of creators with a whole new meta. the details have sort of faded away and now the craft is not in knowing the equipment and how to use it, but how you use it creatively

we're going to see a whole new generation of builders who've never seen or written a line of code build incredible things

note_tweet.text:
codebases have always contained slop. we have always been okay with this because code rarely needs to be perfect, outside of mission critical "hard" (eg embedded) software. 

swe is a unique form of engineering because you're often building something that constantly evolves and is almost organic - user tastes change, your mental models evolve, and features come and go.

admittedly, i and many others who've been coding for a long time were initially (like back in 2024) skeptical that agents would write production code. "but what about all the slop that would enter our beautiful codebase?". 

well, even before, we had human slop, and there was a lot of it! if we're being truthful, most people call "code i didn't write" slop. the reality is that 99% of people (i include myself in that number) don't even know what Good Code looks like, let alone be capable of writing it. i would propose that Good Code is:

• correct
• bug free
• fast and cost efficient to run

it has always been exceedingly difficult and expensive to write truly Good Code, because for the longest time (maybe @bendlang will change that), code was not something you could cheaply and formally guarantee to have all 3 of these properties. this is why writing hard software is much more difficult and expensive, because depending on the use case, you may only get one chance and so you have to be right from the start.

but the vast majority of software we use does not need to be Good Code to provide value to users. in fact, it is very likely that most software we use is not formally verifiable! we accepted some bugs in exchange for velocity and progress, so we rely on tests and o11y instead and have adopted a more incremental approach. this is a good thing! 

agents help us move faster, and if you're open to the idea, are capable of helping us write better code. it won't be Good Code (that is still expensive), but it is likely to be much better on average at scale. 

the new craft of swe is to figure out how to do this. it's your job now! if your productivity with and without agents is not significantly different, you're doing something wrong. but it's not too late to embrace it and use it as an opportunity to learn a whole new skill tree

this is the entrypoint into your most basic agentic loop: verification. it means giving your agent the ability to verify its own work, most commonly by actually running and interacting with it like a real user would. whether your interface is a cli/api/ui/whatever, you want to start here so that your agents can close the loop. if you want you can even have your agents model the problem in TLA+ and attempt to verify if you have things like state machine bugs.

the point is to give yourself confidence in the agents' work by them producing some kind of artifact that proves that 1) that the work is correct, 2) that it matches what you intended, and 3) is easier to review than reading the whole PR. most commonly this would be a video and/or screenshots for UI work.

everything else like skill packs are really bonus and optional, all you need is a way for your agents to verify their own work to start using them more autonomously. some caveats are that not all domains can be verified easily yet, and that verification is just approximation and can still be wrong. it's no different than trusting that a human actually ran the code they wrote and trusting it

so start here!

the 2 things you should know to cut through all the noise:

1. you need to give your agent a way to verify its own work (i just posted about this so won't rehash)
2. your codebase is memory

the 2nd is not new either, we have always had lint rules, compilers with good diagnostics and strong type systems, LSPs, etc to help us write better code. there is no difference when agents write the code instead, you just need more of them, and stronger ones.

forget rules and skills. you can add those later.

yes, your codebase is a form of memory to agents! agents love extending what already exists. so every nit and every annoyance you've ever seen, every mistake and bad pattern you observe from agents, needs to turn into a constraint, or the agents will just keep repeating those same mistakes like a virus in your code. then you keep observing and repeating this process until your codebase is locked down enough that even agents with little context can one shot a high quality PR.

an even better direction is to refactor/rewrite your code such that agent anti-patterns become categorically impossible. use type systems to your advantage, use libraries/frameworks that reduce the architectural search space, or heck, create your own framework like we did for grok bot and design high quality primitives and well thought out APIs

note_tweet.text:
how do you trust your agents' work more? copy this post/link and give it to your @bot or agent!

1. codebase improvements: this is just good software engineering - better architecture, stronger types and invariants, clear boundaries. agents love to copy what exists and take the shortest path, so make the easy thing the right thing. categorically eliminate problems through code and you won't need to think about it again.
2. static analysis: lint rules, tests, CI, verification (eg TLA+). very token efficient ways to catch issues ahead of time.
3. prose: comments, rules, AGENTS.md, skills - anything that can't be enforced and requires agent judgment. use it minimally, but do use /create-verification-skill.
4. human review: the hardest to scale. at the rate agents land code, it's pretty much impossible to thoroughly review every PR, so spend that effort on the highest leverage point, designing an environment where agents do the right thing by default.

this forms an inverse pyramid: you want most of your effort at the top, least at the bottom. codebase improvements are deterministic, making it more token efficient, and lets you sleep more soundly at night.

install https://t.co/u9xIlN3eN0 and create a new Project:
1. look through my slack/chat messages and code review comments where i've given feedback on PRs, code, architecture
2. use /recall on my past transcripts to learn how i steer agents
3. /poteto-mode use /correct and /architect on past commits to find the most common pitfalls agents fall into, then propose a plan to rearchitect the code i own so it's more agent friendly. answer open questions with prototyping rather than defer to me, and back the plan with real data. 
4. before you begin, use /sharpen + /in-your-own-words and confirm this prompt with me

note_tweet.text:
pstack v0.15.27 ships with a new skill /create-formal-verification-skill! 

it's still in beta, and similar to /create-verification-skill, this is a meta-skill that creates a new skill and formal verification suite based on the characteristics you want to verify. for example, you may want to model state machines and systems with concurrency using TLA+, or use kani in rust to check for undefined behavior. 

if you're new to formal verification, think of it as mathematically proving properties and invariants (something that must always be true) or "laws" of your system. usually, this means modeling your programs in a separate language like with TLA+ and then running the solver on that spec. newer approaches like with kani and @bendlang take a different approach where there is no separate language: you write kani in rust, and bend in bend (it's also a programming language, and the proofs are written as laws and expressed in its type system).

historically formal verification never reached mainstream status because of the difficulty in modeling and writing proofs. it's quite difficult to model your business requirements and keep them in sync! but i expect that we will see more innovation in formal verification in the future as being able to formally verifiy that the code does what you intended gives your agents superpowers in writing correct software.

in the meantime though, i've been experimenting with modeling our code with TLA+ and have already found several bugs with the skill created by /create-formal-verification-skill. 

try it out and let me know how it goes!

note_tweet.text:
so many gems and great tips in this talk from @yminsky about how to improve your codebase for agents

• agents thrive on feedback, and types are one of the best kinds 
• make illegal states unrepresentable with types, and it enforces global rules across your codebase
• property based tests, fuzzing, and even full-system deterministic simulation testing
• expect tests: just print stuff out and capture it in the test. makes behavior legible. it's very similar to how compilers have fixture tests, it reduces the review surface area
• formal methods used to be very expensive: seL4 is about 8,700 lines of C and took around 25 person-years, with 23 lines of proof for every line of C code, but agents change the roi

We are terminating Chris Degnan for unethical conduct involving Cognition.

The last few months have seen incredible progress in AI capabilities. San Francisco has flourished as new companies that solve new, more ambitious problems are finding great success. Generally, it is a wonderful time to be building.

We at @FactoryAI have seen overwhelming interest in our model-agnostic coding agents and our software factory product. Our team has 10x’d in size, while our revenue has 100x’d year over year. This momentum has been unprecedented.

A much larger competitor, Cognition (makers of Devin) has fallen behind us on the capabilities that matter most to customers: cost, quality, and security. Instead of competing in the market, Cognition engineers feigned interviews with us to pry information about our product. Not finding what they were looking for, Cognition has decided to throw their weight and money at people with direct knowledge of our most confidential plans.

It feels as though ethics is being thrown out of the window in the AI era. People are willing to do anything, including exploiting privileged information and violating ethical boundaries. I think this is unique to our time, and I don’t think it’s right. Integrity still matters.

Yesterday, I made the decision to immediately terminate Christopher Degnan’s roles as a Board Observer and Advisor to Factory, after over a year of service.

Prior to this decision, Chris told me he had a casual conversation with an executive at Cognition AI. When I questioned his intentions, he reassured me that ethics aside, he had “made too much money” and was “too lazy to go work for Cognition,” which I trusted and believed.

On Monday, Chris spent time advising the Factory team on a handful of confidential board-level matters. That evening, he called me to say that the conversation that was initially described as casual and one-off was actually formal and recurring. For weeks, while he sat in our board meetings and advised our leadership team, he was also confiding with executives of our largest competitor. Chris was subject to confidentiality obligations in connection with his work with Factory. We do not know the extent of the information he shared, but it puts his timely questions about our product roadmap and what the parity gap involves into a new light.

It is sad to sever a relationship with someone who has been a trusted advisor - and even a close friend -  for over a year. But Chris’s conduct is unacceptable to me. Trust in Board Membership is one of the sacred bonds in the Silicon Valley, one that helps the startup ecosystem thrive. With it comes an enormous responsibility. That trust was violated.

Competition is good. I respect and in many cases admire our competitors. San Francisco is a beautiful, singular place where the bold and ambitious go to defy the norms and precedents of the past. But certain principles that must remain. Violating ethics to seek advantage turns what should be positive-sum into zero-sum.

We all love technology. And we all love to compete. But we must hold ourselves to a higher standard. The future of software engineering comes with abundance that will impact every person on Earth. Building that future comes with immense responsibility. We must build and compete with integrity.

note_tweet.text:
volume does matter
look, i get it. if you were an engineer before agents came along, you're rightfully skeptical about lines of code and number of PRs being used as a metric for any kind of productivity. and i agree! or at least, i used to. for ease of explanation i will talk about this from the perspective as being an engineer on a large team of at least 50. 

volume didn't matter before because we focused on impact. you could have high impact even with a few PRs: for example you could make a one line config change and save the company millions of dollars.  

but before agents, the times where i saw volume come into the conversation were for the outliers. on the negative end you might have someone who is struggling to perform, on the other end you might have someone who was a "coding machine" archetype. a coding machine was someone who could just lock themselves in a room and emerge with a stack of PRs that solve a huge number of problems. so volume did matter, but only at the tail ends of the distribution, and combined with impact.

if you've ever worked at a large tech company before, you'll get what i mean. the thing about agents is that big tech co problems are now small-medium co problems as well. 

how do agents change this calculus? well, everyone now has the ability to become a coding machine. you have incredibly capable frontier models that can write code better than any of us, at a rate much faster than we can. in this world, if you're still producing the same number of PRs as before, why wouldn't you pause to wonder why you're not being more productive? alien intelligence is here, and yet you can't outship a human coding machine?

this brings me back to why i keep talking about trust (https://t.co/7fzYZV8LGH). if you haven't put in the work to trust your agent's output, it is very difficult to scale up your productivity. 

and yes, this approach does require more tokens, but i think about this in terms of cost per intelligence. before agents, this cost was very high - you needed to hire many software engineers with high 6 figure salaries to do the work. tokens are still expensive today, but are likely to get cheaper over time (https://t.co/gTBZx7pl14) factoring in the cost of intelligence. what looks exorbitant today will likely be affordable in 6 moths to a year. a single engineer with agents can do the work of tens if not hundreds of engineers, at a fraction of the cost.

the reality that i don't think has hit yet is that job of the software engineer has truly changed. our job is not merely to produce software any longer (well tbh it was never only about the code, but bear with me for the sake of the explanation), but the machine that writes the software. this idea of a software factory, or a Michelin kitchen as i like to call it, is still a topic of research. and it's the type of stuff i like to share, not to flex, but to show you what's possible when you put a lot of rigor into using agents at scale

volume does matter
look, i get it. if you were poasting before bots came along, you’re rightfully skeptical about poast count and impressions being used as a metric for any kind of influence. and i agree! or at least, i used to. for ease of explanation i will talk about this from the perspective of someone who’s been poasting long enough to remember when it was called twitter.

volume didn’t matter before because we focused on impact. you could have high impact even with a few poasts: for example you could drop one banger at 9am on a tuesday and it would do more for you than a year of gm poasting.

but before bots, the times where i saw volume come into the conversation were for the outliers. on the negative end you might have someone who poasts once a quarter and wonders why the algo hates them. on the other end you might have someone who was a “poasting machine” archetype. a poasting machine was someone who could just lock themselves in a room (never touching grass) and emerge with a stack of threads, quote tweets, and ratios that somehow all landed. so volume did matter, but only at the tail ends of the distribution, and combined with impact.

if you’ve ever run a big account before, you’ll get what i mean. the thing about bots is that big account problems are now small account problems as well.

how do bots change this calculus? well, everyone now has the ability to become a poasting machine. you have incredibly capable bots that can write poasts better than any of us, at a rate much faster than we can. in this world, if you’re still poasting the same amount as before, why wouldn’t you pause to wonder why you’re not being more prolific? alien intelligence is here, and yet you can’t outpoast a human reply guy?

this brings me back to why i keep talking about trust. if you haven’t put in the work to trust your bot’s output, it is very difficult to make number go up.

and yes, this approach does require more tokens, but i think about this in terms of cost per intelligence. before bots, this cost was very high: you needed to hire ghostwriters and a social media team to keep the timeline fed. tokens are still expensive today, but are likely to get cheaper over time factoring in the cost of intelligence. what looks exorbitant today will likely be affordable in 6 months to a year. a single poaster with bots can do the work of tens if not hundreds of social media managers, at a fraction of the cost.

the reality that i don’t think has hit yet is that the job of the poaster has truly changed. our job is not merely to produce poasts any longer (well tbh it was never only about the poasts, but bear with me for the sake of the explanation), but the machine that writes the poasts. this idea of a poasting factory, or a bot farm as i like to call it, is still a topic of research. and it’s the type of stuff i like to share, not to flex, but to show you what’s possible when you put a lot of rigor into using bots at scale

I've been thinking more about the this reply and I think I figured it out. 

> how did you trust it before when humans wrote it?

you mostly didn't, not really. you trusted the tests, the fact that it was already in production somewhere similar, the author's track record, and the reality that most of the time the bug would show up in monitoring before it became a real problem. the diff was honestly a ritual more than a guarantee. we pretended like line-level review was a safety net because we didn't have better options and the volume was low enough that it felt manageable. 

but agents just make the old ritual obvious. once you're landing thousands of changes a month the idea that someone is carefully reading every diff starts being theater. 

trusting agent output is the same problem as trusting human output, just with higher throughput. I think the answer is still to stop treating the change as the thing you trust and start treating the environment as the thing you trust. if an agent can run the code, drive the ui, check the invariants, and get blocked by the same constraints a human would, the fact that it wrote the patch matters less. 

every time you find yourself wanting to open the diff "just to make sure," that's signal that something in the system is still relying on human eyeballs instead of a hard constraint.

the code review as we know it is already on the way out. most of what we call review today will turn into risk scoring and continuous verification. low and medium risk work will land after agents and checks have already exercised it. 

humans will still be involved, but not by reading patches. they'll just be deciding what outcomes matter, whats not allowed to break, and which constraints are worth making permanent. 

the job now is to continuously make the system good enough that you don't need the diff to feel safe.

an even better direction is to refactor/rewrite your code such that agent anti-patterns become categorically impossible. use type systems to your advantage, use libraries/frameworks that reduce the architectural search space, or heck, create your own framework like we did for grok bot and design high quality primitives and well thought out APIs

as models get smarter, i expect most of pstack skills to compress into short principles or workflows (a generic list of steps) and that i will be able to delete a few of them. 

how it works is that /poteto-mode contains a short index of available principles and tells agents "In your reply, name each principle that shaped a decision and the specific choice it changed." this is why you'll often see a Principles Named or Used section at the end of the agent's response

many of these principles were extracted from my sessions correcting agents since the start of this year. some are inspired by problems i see people talk about, like Attack the Premise, inspired by @VictorTaelin's post https://t.co/qTGVfoKSyD

you can also use the principles as skills if you want greater control, by invoking /principle-<name> 

https://t.co/wuTWsflVN3

note_tweet.text:
ban and delete most if not all code comments!

agents love copying what already exists. a seemingly harmless comment explaining some temporary workaround is one of the worst viruses you can have in your codebase. like a weed it'll spread quickly as a tool for agents to quickly get their job done. before you know it, your codebase is overrun with hacks and stale comments. just one more workaround bro 

you can use pstack's /no-comments skill as a weedkiller. it'll seek out useless comments while keeping the ones that actually should exist (like explaining a browser quirk), and figure out how to solve them on a first principles basis

here's a prompt you can try asking @bot:

create a project agent that uses /poteto-mode to spawn a /swarm to use /no-comments and identify useless code comments we can prune in my repo. come back with a high level plan of which of these workarounds would be best solved by refactoring and which we can straight up delete

i've been bashing on "software is dead" for a while now. it's probably time for me to start sharing what i think will happen instead as well

there's so much to unpack, so i'm going to split it into a series of a few parts

today i'll start with part 1 - jevons paradox

story time - let's rewind to the industrial revolution, when steam engines powered all the factories, railways and effectively the economy

but steam engines had to burn coal - a lot of them. there's a limited amount of coal available, so people started to optimize the steam engines to use less coal

that's when the counter-intuitive thing happened - when steam engines used less coal, the industry actually ended up using more coal in total

how?? what jevons found and documented in his book was - when steam engines used less coal, they became cheaper to deploy and run, and hence became economically viable in more places, so the total demand rose significantly as a result

when the barrier of entry to create software is significantly reduced, the same will happen - software will become much cheaper and more accessible

hesitant to pay $100/month for the adobe suite today? well, what if it becomes $10 lifetime purchase?

sick of so many mobile apps having a paywall? well, what if the entire app store is $5/month all-you-can-eat?

the price point for each individual piece of software will drop, but the software economy as a whole will become a lot larger because of the rising consumption demand

so many more people and businesses will get access to software that's too costly for them to use today

so many more people who aren't developing software today will be able to participate, create, help grow the economy and make a living out of it

software is nowhere near "dead". it's just about to take off

not on my most optimistic dreams I expected someone to "get it" as much as Giulio does and yes that's the point

today models are already incredibly capable, and they're smart enough to build infinitely complex software, but mistakes accumulate, and it reaches a level of tech debt where progress stalls. if there only was some magic way to tell the agent "hey, this is wrong, try again" until no bugs are left, then, there would be no limits to the complexity of software that AI can build

that's what Bend does!!

sure, it takes more time (and tokens) to solve the same problem, but that's exactly because writing correct code takes time! Bend refuses any incorrect output, and that's what you WANT to happen. merging bugs give you an illusion of progress, but it bites later

I for one am not using any other language anymore. if Bend is an absolute failure, at least it is the language I'll be using for my own projects moving forward

(and Bend in Bend is already in progress)

note_tweet.text:
Give your agent a way to verify its work. This can dramatically improve the quality of output.

With this process in place, Claude Code was able to write 90%+ of its code itself. When generating software at a faster rate than you can review it, the bottleneck shifts to proving that it works. @bcherny and team invested enough in verification, we've been able to move fast while maintaining stability.

Code reviews aren't going away, but you need to think of it differently. One human reading through line-by-line is no longer going to work as a gate, it needs to evolve into a multi-layered verification system, built with fast deterministic feedback loops for your agents. 

This is where e2e tests, feature maps (as @poteto has been advocating), property tests and multi-agent adversarial reviews come in. These all provide opportunities to catch errors early and fix them before things get out of hand.

You don't have enough eyeballs for the amount of code being written so your focus needs to be on product intent, risk assessment and evaluating evidence rather than reviewing code. Delegate the code checking work to your automated tests, scale your approvals based on risk, and turn your test failures into living evaluations. This approach helps maintain speed without losing reliability.

Let the agents do what they do best and let you focus on what makes you irreplaceable: judgement, direction, and ownership. We tried to capture how we handle code review and verification in this writeup. Hopefully it's helpful.
